newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin government bickers about Bewag sale.
newsitem.headline: Berlin government bickers about Bewag sale.

text.p: Plans to privatise Berlin power utility Bewag were teetering near collapse on Thursday after one more international bidder pulled out of the race, leaving government officials to bicker about what to do next.

Berlin city finance minister Annette Fugmann-Heesing has threatened to suspend bidding for Berliner Kraft und Licht AG (Bewag) if all foreign bidders dropped out of the race, having made no secret that she wants a foreign group to buy the stake.
The process moved one step closer to collapse after British group PowerGen joined U.S.-based Enron in deciding not to make a bid for the 50.8 percent stake in Bewag.
That leaves U.S. group Southern Corp as the sole foreign group facing off against a German consortium of VIAG AG and Veba AG for control of the utility.
VIAG and Veba's PreussenElektra und Bayernwerk units each own a 10 percent stake in Bewag and control 14 percent of Bewag's supervisory board.

The precarious situation has put Fugmann-Heesing's Social Democrat Party (SPD) on a collision course with its Christian Democrat (CDU) coalition partner, which clearly favours selling the stake to a German group.
The government is coming under ever greater pressure to wrap up talks as it needs to sell at least 25.8 percent of its 50.8 percent by the end of February for financial reasons.
The SPD has been very critical of CDU comments that any decisions concerning Bewag may not be made abroad,
Rudolf Hartung, general secretary of the local SPD party, attacked senior CDU official Klaus Landowsky for saying harmful things about Bewag.
Landowsky is head of Berlin- Hannoverische Hypothekenbank AG which is part of Bankgesellschaft Berlin.

A spokesman for Landowsky rejected the criticism and said foreign bidders were not adequately informed about the intricacies of the sale, which would leave them only with a majority stake but not a majority on the supervisory board.

Industry sources say foreign bidders were very worried by existing commitments by the state to PreussenElektra and Bayernwerk that promise them three seats on the supervisory board. This was the main reason many dropped out of the race, the sources have said.
Neither Enron nor PowerGen commented officially on their reasons for pulling out of the race. Government officials declined to comment officially on the negotiations and the possible next steps.
